A.explanation: Current about $0.45 \text{ A}$ leaves about $7.1 \text{ V}$ across the variable resistor, giving $R \approx 16 \, \Omega$.

B.explanation: This adds the $20 \, \Omega$ device to $16 \, \Omega$ instead of giving the variable resistance alone.

C.explanation: This uses total resistance $V^2/P$ incorrectly for the $4.0 \text{ W}$ device rather than using $P=I^2R$ for the $20 \, \Omega$ part.

D.explanation: This assumes the full $16 \text{ V}$ is across the $20 \, \Omega$ device when finding current, ignoring the series voltage drop.

hints: Notice the $20 \, \Omega$ device and variable resistor are in series with the $16 \text{ V}$ battery, so they share the same current but split the $16 \text{ V}$.
Use $P=I^2R$ with $P=4.0 \text{ W}$ and $R=20 \, \Omega$ to find the series current, then find the voltage across the $20 \, \Omega$ device.
Subtract the device voltage from $16 \text{ V}$ to get the variable resistor voltage, then use $R=V/I$ for the variable resistor.
walkthrough: The series loop has the same current $I$ through the $20 \, \Omega$ device and the variable resistor $R$, with total e.m.f. $16 \text{ V}$ and negligible internal resistance.
Power in the fixed device is $P=I^2R$, so $4.0 = I^2 \times 20$ giving $I^2 = 0.20$ and $I = \sqrt{0.20} \approx 0.447 \text{ A}$.
Voltage across the device is $V_{device}=IR = 0.447 \times 20 \approx 8.94 \text{ V}$.
By Kirchhoff voltage law, voltage across the variable resistor is $V_R = 16 - V_{device} \approx 16 - 8.94 = 7.06 \text{ V}$.
Hence $R = V_R/I \approx 7.06/0.447 \approx 15.8 \, \Omega$, about $16 \, \Omega$. This is option A.
